briefing.text: Check how ER_STATUS is coded before comparing groups: the library reports that the column description line in data_clinical_patient.txt says 1 = negative and 0 = positive (reverse of the usual convention). Read the '#' description line yourself, cross-tabulate ER_STATUS against ER_PERCENT_POSITIVE (ER-negative tumours should have ~0% positive cells), define ER-positive explicitly from what the metadata says, and resolve or document any status/percent disagreements.
briefing.reason: Getting the coding wrong flips the direction of the comparison and therefore the label.

briefing.text: PROLIFERATION_SCORE is a sample-level variable and a patient may have several samples (e.g. primary and metastasis). Count samples per PATIENT_ID and tabulate SAMPLE_TYPE; if patients have multiple samples, analyse one sample per patient (preferably the primary tumour) or aggregate per patient, or use a mixed model with a patient random effect, and check whether a primary-only analysis gives the same result.
briefing.reason: Naive sample-level tests pseudoreplicate and over-weight some patients.

briefing.text: Before testing, count missing/blank/sentinel/out-of-range values in PROLIFERATION_SCORE, ER_STATUS and ER_PERCENT_POSITIVE, and count sample PATIENT_IDs that do not join to the patient table. Exclude or document these, inspect the score distribution for skew, and use a rank-based test (Mann-Whitney) or robust regression alongside any t-test.
briefing.reason: Silent data-quality problems and skew can bias the group comparison.

briefing.text: Cross-tabulate PROCESSING_BATCH by ER group and compare proliferation-score distributions by batch. If batch is associated with ER, adjust for it (regression covariate or within-batch comparison); if batch is fully confounded with ER, say so, since the comparison may then be unresolvable.
briefing.reason: Batch effects can create or mask a proliferation difference between ER groups.

briefing.text: Expression-derived scores depend on TUMOR_PURITY. Correlate proliferation score with purity and compare purity between ER groups; if relevant, fit proliferation ~ ER + purity (+ batch) and report crude and adjusted estimates.
briefing.reason: Purity differences between ER groups can confound the comparison.

briefing.text: SITE (enrolling hospital) and SAMPLE_TYPE (primary vs metastasis) may differ in ER mix and in proliferation/assay handling. Compare the ER effect within SITE and within SAMPLE_TYPE strata; if the crude and stratified/adjusted directions disagree (Simpson-type reversal), prefer the adjusted estimate and report both.
briefing.reason: A crude difference can be confounded or even reversed by site or sample type.

briefing.text: The hypothesis is directional (ER-positive higher). Report the direction and size of the difference (mean/median difference with a confidence interval), not just a p-value. A clear, robust difference in the opposite direction is evidence against the hypothesis (label False), not a reason for 'Not verifiable'; 'Not verifiable' is for when the relevant variables are absent or the comparison truly cannot be resolved.
briefing.reason: Prevents mislabelling an opposite-direction result as True or Not verifiable.

shared_assumptions: Both teams treat sample type as a nuisance covariate (adjusting or restricting to primaries) and assume one common ER effect, although team A reports opposite-signed estimates in primaries (-4.87) and metastases (+2.6). Neither tested an ER x sample-type interaction, and neither showed whether the ER mix differs by sample type.

Both assume batch is a pre-ER technical confounder that should be adjusted for. Neither checked whether batch could instead be a downstream or collider variable, or whether the all-sample estimate depends on how the batch levels are modelled. The crude p is ~0.1 and the adjusted p is ~0.05.

Both assume all 302 patients are in scope for an ER comparison. The patient table has a SEX column that includes males, and neither team reported the sex distribution or the cancer type, or checked whether the ER effect is the same in both sexes.
unused_evidence: SEX (patient table): it is not used as a covariate or as a scope filter. If sex is unbalanced across ER groups, or if it interacts with ER, the pooled estimate could change.

data_clinical_supplement.txt (ECOG_PS, BMI, FOLLOW_UP_MONTHS): neither team says it used these. They are probably irrelevant to the hypothesis, but neither team confirmed they are balanced or free of sentinel values.
ER_PERCENT_POSITIVE as a continuous measure: team B ran a Spearman correlation but did not report it. It gives a dose-response check on direction that does not depend on the binary coding.
HYPOXIA_SCORE and the serum labs: not used. They could serve as negative controls for batch or site artefacts (does the batch shift appear in every assay score?).
unresolved_weak_points: Team A: the metastasis subgroup points the opposite way. This was reported but not resolved, and team A promoted the primary-only analysis to the main evidence after seeing the results.

Team B: the effect is small and borderline (adjusted p~0.049, crude p~0.096). This was reported, not resolved. Neither team checked how sensitive the result is to the choice of covariate set or to influential points.
second_readings: 'Patients with ER-positive tumours' could mean all patients, using whatever sample they have (primary or metastasis), or primary-tumour status only. The two readings give estimates of different strength and opposite sign in the subgroups.

'Contradicts' could mean a significantly lower ER+ score, or only a point estimate in the wrong direction. A null or borderline difference does not support the hypothesis, but whether that is 'False' depends on this reading. The teams should state which threshold they used, and why.
challenge.verdict: I moderately trust the agreed direction (ER-positive lower). Both teams decoded the reversed ER coding correctly and checked it. But the evidence is borderline (crude p~0.1), it rests partly on a primary-only subset chosen after seeing the data, and metastases point the other way. The 'False' label needs the interaction and robustness checks before it is reported.

questions.question: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Fit proliferation ~ ER * SAMPLE_TYPE (plus batch) on all samples, and cross-tabulate ER by sample type. Is the interaction material? If it is, does reporting the primary-only estimate as the main evidence still fit a hypothesis stated about patients in general, or does your method need to change?
QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Tabulate SEX by ER status and repeat the ER comparison within each sex. Does the sex mix or a sex-specific effect change your direction or your confidence?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Regress proliferation on ER_PERCENT_POSITIVE among ER-positive patients, and check HYPOXIA_SCORE for the same batch shifts as a negative control. Do these support a real ER-related difference rather than a batch or assay artefact?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: You report ER+ lower within B2-B4. What happens in B1? Also fit an ER * PROCESSING_BATCH interaction and a leave-one-batch-out analysis. Does the borderline adjusted estimate hold up when any single batch is removed?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Estimate the ER effect separately in metastases and in primaries, and test the ER x SAMPLE_TYPE interaction. If the two disagree in sign, how does that affect a 'False' call for all patients?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Check SEX by ER status, and the supplement variables (ECOG_PS, BMI) for imbalance and sentinel values. Does adding or stratifying on them move the adjusted estimate across your decision threshold?

In observational comparisons, when a two-group difference in means reverses sign between subgroups (e.g. primary tumour vs metastasis samples), what is the recommended way to test and report effect modification versus a pooled adjusted estimate?
questions.why: Both teams pooled or restricted the data without testing for interaction, and the conclusion depends on which population is meant.

questions.question: What are the standard practices for handling processing-batch effects in gene expression signature scores when batch is partially associated with the group of interest (covariate adjustment, ComBat-style correction, or within-batch comparison), and what are the known pitfalls of each?
questions.why: The significance of the all-sample effect changes with batch adjustment, so whether that adjustment is valid matters for the label.

findings.question: In observational comparisons, when a two-group difference in means reverses sign between subgroups (e.g. primary tumour vs metastasis samples), what is the recommended way to test and report effect modification versus a pooled adjusted estimate?
findings.answer: NOT SETTLED BY WEB: every search and contents call failed with HTTP 502/403 from the gateway, so no page was read. From background knowledge only: fit one model with an ER x SAMPLE_TYPE interaction term and test it. Report the ER effect in each stratum with CIs, together with the interaction test (Knol & VanderWeele 2012 reporting guidance). If the effect reverses sign across strata, a single pooled adjusted estimate is misleading: it averages opposite effects and depends on the stratum mix. Choose and state the target population. For a tumour-level hypothesis this is usually primary tumours, one sample per patient. Interaction tests have low power, so a non-significant interaction does not prove the effect is the same across strata.

findings.question: What are the standard practices for handling processing-batch effects in gene expression signature scores when batch is partially associated with the group of interest (covariate adjustment, ComBat-style correction, or within-batch comparison), and what are the known pitfalls of each?
findings.answer: NOT SETTLED BY WEB: the gateway failed (HTTP 403), so no page was read. From background knowledge only: the preferred approach is to put batch as a covariate in the outcome model (score ~ ER + batch), or to compare within batch and combine the strata. Pitfalls: (1) Correcting with ComBat or similar before testing, without group in the model, can remove real group signal. With group in the model, an unbalanced design gives overconfident, inflated significance and extra false positives (Nygaard, Rødland & Hovig 2016, Biostatistics). (2) Covariate adjustment cannot separate batch from group when they are fully confounded, and it loses precision when they are strongly associated. (3) Within-batch comparison loses power and excludes batches that hold only one group. If the ER effect keeps its direction but loses significance after adjustment, that points to lost precision or partial confounding, not to a reversal. Always cross-tabulate batch by group first (Leek et al. 2010, Nat Rev Genet).
